sections.h2: How is Oklahoma organized when you sell a house here?
sections.html:
Oklahoma has 77 counties, and almost every step of a house sale touches a county office. The state also counts 597 municipalities, made up of 164 cities and 433 towns. Cities carry the larger share of the population, but deeds, tax bills and court cases all run through the county where the land sits.

The counties differ a great deal in size. Oklahoma County is the most populous at 822,125 people, while Cimarron County in the panhandle has 2,059. Some cities cross lines too. Oklahoma City lies mostly in Oklahoma County with parts in Canadian, Cleveland and Pottawatomie counties, and Tulsa spills into Osage, Rogers and Wagoner counties. If your house sits near one of those edges, confirm which county holds your parcel before you call anyone.

For a quick look at the guides we keep for individual places, start with our Oklahoma guides by city and county and the county list further down this page.

sections.h2: When are Oklahoma property taxes due, and what happens if they are late?
sections.html:
Ad valorem taxes become due on November 1 each year. The whole bill turns delinquent on January 1 unless at least half has been paid by then. If the first half is in, the rest must be paid before April 1. State law allows no more than two installments, and mortgage servicers pay the full year in one payment before January 1.

Your county treasurer collects the money and your county assessor sets the value, so those are the two offices to call about a bill or a valuation. Both sit in the county courthouse. Our Oklahoma property tax guide walks through appeals and selling with tax due, and the county guides below show where the offices are.

Unpaid taxes do not block a sale by themselves. They are normally paid out of the proceeds at closing, so ask the title company for a payoff figure early.

sections.h2: What does the homestead exemption do for a seller?
sections.html:
It takes $1,000 off the assessed value of an owner-occupied home, which trims the yearly tax bill by a modest amount. State law exempts each homestead from ad valorem tax to the extent of $1,000 of assessed valuation.

It does not stop a sale. Read more on our Oklahoma homestead exemption page, and ask the assessor whether your exemption is on file.

sections.h2: How much does the deed transfer cost in Oklahoma?
sections.html:
Oklahoma charges a documentary stamp tax of 75 cents for each $500 of consideration, or any fraction of $500. It applies to a deed when the value conveyed, not counting any lien that stays on the property, is more than $100. The tax attaches when the deed is signed and delivered to the buyer.

As a worked example, a $200,000 sale equals 400 units of $500, so the stamp comes to $300. The statute itself does not say which side pays, so the purchase contract and the closing agent settle that. Recording the deed is a separate county clerk step, and each county sets out its own fees. The clerk pages for Grady County and McClain County show how that looks locally.

Income tax on any gain is a different matter and depends on how long you owned the house. See our Oklahoma capital gains page for the order of operations.

sections.h2: How does foreclosure work in Oklahoma, and how long do you have?
sections.html:
Oklahoma allows both court foreclosure and non-judicial foreclosure, so the route depends on what the mortgage says. Under state law, a lender can hold a power of sale only if the mortgage says so in bold, underlined language. Most home loans without that statement go through a court case that ends with a sale ordered by a judge, usually run by the county sheriff.

When a power of sale exists, the lender must first send a notice of intent by certified mail. That notice gives the owner 35 days from the date it is sent to cure the default and reinstate the loan. A homeowner can also elect court foreclosure instead. To do that, the owner sends a certified letter to the lender and records a copy with the county clerk at least ten days before the power of sale date, and the owner must say the property is a homestead.

The real length varies from loan to loan. Our Oklahoma sheriff sale page covers what happens after the judgment.

sections.h2: What happens with an inherited house in Oklahoma?
sections.html:
If the owner died with the house in a sole name and no beneficiary designation, a probate case in district court usually has to run before anyone can sign a deed. The Oklahoma Bar Association describes the main steps:

  • A petition is filed, and a will petition is set for hearing between 10 and 30 days after filing.
  • The court names a personal representative, who receives letters after taking an oath.
  • The representative files an inventory within two months of appointment unless the court waives it.
  • Notice to creditors goes out within two months of the letters, with a claims date at least two months away.

The Bar Association also notes there is no statute of limitation for filing a probate. A house can wait in a dead owner's name, but taxes and upkeep keep adding up in the meantime.

Selling needs authority. If the will gives a power of sale, the court must still confirm the sale unless every heir has waived confirmation. Without a power of sale, the representative can ask the court for permission with written consent from all heirs and devisees, which allows the sale without a later confirmation hearing. If the heirs do not all agree, the longer procedure of 58 O.S. section 380 and following applies, including appraisal and court confirmation.

Some houses skip probate. A surviving joint tenant can end a deceased owner's interest by filing the documents named in the statute, and a transfer on death deed names who receives the house. See our probate page, transfer on death deed page and estate tax page. Oklahoma has no estate tax for deaths after 2009, and the stepped-up basis for heirs can lower the tax bill when the house is sold.

sections.h2: What if the house has tenants?
sections.html:
A sale does not cancel a lease, so the tenant situation travels with the house. For a month to month or at-will tenancy, either side can end it with written notice at least 30 days before the termination date. A tenancy shorter than month to month needs at least 7 days of written notice. The period starts when the notice is served as the statute describes.

  • Check whether each lease is written, oral or month to month.
  • Collect rent records and any deposit paperwork before you list or talk to buyers.
  • Ask the buyer in writing whether they want the tenant to stay or the house delivered empty.

Our landlord and tenant page, eviction notice page and eviction process page explain the timelines in detail.

sections.h2: What does a cash sale as-is mean here?
sections.html:
It means the buyer takes the house in its current condition and pays with cash or funds that need no mortgage approval, so there is usually no lender appraisal or repair list to clear. You still sign a purchase contract, the deed is still stamped and recorded, and a title company or closing attorney still handles the paperwork.

Cash does not erase liens. Back taxes, an unpaid mortgage or a judgment lien come out of the proceeds at closing, or the title work will flag them first. If a probate or a tenant stands in the way, that has to be sorted out whatever form of payment is used.

The buyer and seller agree in the contract who handles closing, whether a title company or a closing attorney. For storm, flood or radon questions, ask a local inspector or your county office.

sections.h2: Which Oklahoma county office should you call first?
sections.html:
Start with the office that matches the question. The assessor handles value and exemptions, the treasurer takes tax payments, the county clerk records deeds, and the district court clerk holds probate and foreclosure files. The sheriff runs forced sales in that county.

  • Tax bill or payoff: county treasurer.
  • Valuation or homestead filing: county assessor.
  • Recording a deed: county clerk.
  • Probate or foreclosure case: district court clerk.

Pick your county below for its guide.

faqs.q: How many counties does Oklahoma have?
faqs.a: Oklahoma has 77 counties, and each one runs its own assessor, treasurer, clerk and sheriff's office. Which county your house sits in decides who you call about taxes and deed recording.

faqs.q: When are Oklahoma property taxes due?
faqs.a: Taxes are due November 1. The bill is delinquent on January 1 unless half or more has been paid, and the second half is due before April 1. A payoff figure from the treasurer or title company shows what is owed.

faqs.q: What is the Oklahoma deed stamp tax?
faqs.a: It is 75 cents for each $500 of consideration, so a $200,000 sale works out to $300. The contract or closing agent decides who pays it.

faqs.q: Can I sell a house that is in foreclosure?
faqs.a: Yes, you can sell before the sheriff's sale date. A power of sale mortgage gives you 35 days from the lender's notice to cure, and a court case ends in a confirmed sale. Talk to the lender and a local attorney about timing.

faqs.q: Does an inherited house have to go through probate?
faqs.a: Usually, if it was in the owner's sole name. A transfer on death deed, a trust or joint tenancy with survivorship can pass it without a full probate. The district court of the right county handles the case.

faqs.q: How much notice does a month to month tenant get?
faqs.a: Oklahoma requires 30 days of written notice to end a month to month tenancy. Shorter tenancies need 7 days.

faqs.q: Do I have to make repairs before a cash sale?
faqs.a: No state rule requires repairs before an as-is sale. The buyer and seller agree on condition in the contract, and liens still have to be paid from the proceeds.
